SW1 Fa0/1 is hardcoded to 100/full. The PC on the other end is on auto. What does the PC settle on, and what's the result?

100/half.
It senses the speed from the signal, but duplex can't be sensed, so it falls back to half at 10/100. The link comes up with a duplex mismatch.
A PC's NIC is hardcoded to 10/full. The switch port is on auto. What does the switch port settle on?

10/half.
The auto side matches whatever speed it senses (10), then falls back to half duplex because it's at 10/100. Speed isn't a fixed default; only duplex is.
One side is hardcoded to 1000/full and the other is on auto. By the fallback rule, what duplex does the auto side pick?

Full.
The fallback is half at 10 and 100, full at 1000 and up. (In practice, gigabit over copper needs negotiation, so many devices won't link at all in this setup.)
Both sides are on auto. The switch port supports 10/100/1000, but the PC's NIC only supports 10/100. What do they settle on?

100/full.
Both sides negotiate, share their capabilities, and pick the best mode they both support. Fallback rules only apply when one side isn't negotiating.
Both sides are on auto and both support 10/100/1000. What do they settle on?
1000/full. Both negotiate and pick the best mode they share.
SW1 Gi0/1 is hardcoded to 100/full. SW2 Gi0/1 is hardcoded to 10/full. What state is the link in?

down/down.
Both sides are hardcoded to different speeds, so neither can decode the other's signal. A true speed mismatch basically only happens when both sides are hardcoded.
SW1 is hardcoded to 100/full. SW2 is hardcoded to 100/half. What happens?

The link comes up at 100 with a duplex mismatch.
SW2 (half) counts collisions and late collisions. SW1 (full) counts CRC errors and runts.
In a duplex mismatch, which errors show up on the half-duplex side, and which on the full-duplex side?

Half side: collisions and late collisions.
Full side: CRC errors and runts, from receiving the half side's chopped-off frames.
A switch port facing a PC shows CRC errors and runts climbing, and zero collisions. Which end is running half duplex?

The PC.
The switch port is the full side: it's receiving the PC's chopped-off frames. The half side is the one counting collisions.
A switch port shows late collisions climbing and a CRC count of 0. Which end is running half duplex?

This port.
Only a port following half-duplex rules counts collisions. On a switched link, late collisions point at this port being the half side of a duplex mismatch.
show interfaces status shows a port at a-half, a-100, with a printer on the other end. What does 'a-' mean, and what's the likely story?

'a-' means the switch reached that value by auto-negotiation, so the switch side isn't hardcoded.
Modern gear doesn't choose half on purpose, so the printer is probably hardcoded and the switch fell back to half: a likely duplex mismatch.
Why can an auto side sense the other end's speed but not its duplex?
Each speed uses a different signal on the wire, so speed can be detected just by listening. Duplex isn't visible in the signal; it's only shared through negotiation. No negotiation, no duplex info.
A cable links fine at 100 Mbps but won't come up at gigabit. Both ends are gig-capable and on auto. Most likely cause?

A damaged pair that 10/100 doesn't use.
10/100 uses two pairs (pins 1, 2, 3, 6). 1000BASE-T uses all four, so a bad pair on pins 4, 5, 7, 8 breaks gig but not 100.
How does full duplex send and receive at the same time at 100 Mbps, versus at 1000 Mbps?

100: one pair sends, a separate pair receives.
1000: all four pairs carry both directions at once. Each end subtracts its own signal from what's on the wire to hear the other side.
What is CSMA/CD, and where is it still used today?

Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection: listen before sending, and if two devices collide, stop, jam, wait a random time, and retry.
Today it's only active on half-duplex ports. Full duplex turns it off.
How does a wired half-duplex port detect a collision?
It hears a signal on its receive pair while it's transmitting on its send pair. Hearing something while talking means a collision.
Why does Wi-Fi use CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD?

A radio can't hear other stations while it's transmitting; its own signal drowns everything out. So Wi-Fi avoids collisions (a random wait before sending) and uses acknowledgments: no ACK means assume a collision and resend.
What's a late collision, and what does it usually point to?

A collision detected after the first 64 bytes of a frame. On a properly built network that shouldn't happen.
Usual causes: a duplex mismatch, or a cable run that's too long.
Why is the minimum Ethernet frame 64 bytes?
So the sender is still transmitting when a collision from the far end of a properly sized network reaches it. With shorter frames, a sender could finish before hearing the collision and never know.
What's the maximum standard Ethernet frame size, and where does the number come from?

1518 bytes = 1500 payload (MTU) + 14 header + 4 FCS.
Anything bigger arriving on a port counts as a giant.
A 9018-byte frame arrives on a port with the default MTU. What counter does it hit?
Giants. It's bigger than the 1518-byte maximum the port accepts. Classic cause: one side sending jumbo frames, the other not configured for them.
A 48-byte frame arrives on a port. What counter does it hit, and what's a common cause?

Runts (under the 64-byte minimum).
Common cause: the full-duplex side of a duplex mismatch receiving frames the half side cut off mid-send.
A Cisco interface is at its default MTU of 1500. The Juniper on the other end shows MTU 1514. Is that a mismatch?
No. Same limit. Juniper's physical MTU includes the 14-byte Ethernet header; Cisco's counts only the payload. Juniper's inet MTU under the unit shows 1500.
A storage network turns on jumbo frames (MTU 9000) on the servers and the NAS. Large transfers fail, small ones work. Most likely problem?
A device in the path is still at MTU 1500, so the big frames get dropped there as giants. Every device in the path has to support jumbo frames.
Why can an MTU mismatch go unnoticed for weeks?

Small packets fit, so pings, SSH, and routing updates all work. Only full-size packets fail, and they're dropped quietly instead of showing up as CRC errors. It surfaces when bulk traffic moves through the path.
Why do jumbo frames speed up big transfers?

Every frame carries roughly the same header overhead. A 9000-byte frame carries six times the data of a 1500-byte one, so the same file needs about a sixth as many frames and headers to send and process.
A user on a 500 Mbps plan sees downloads at 62 MB/s and says they're getting an eighth of their speed. Are they?
No. 62 MB/s x 8 = 496 Mbps. They're getting essentially the full plan. Megabytes vs megabits.
Roughly how long does a 40 GB file take over a 100 Mbps link, ignoring overhead?

40 GB x 8 = 320 Gb = 320,000 Mb.
320,000 / 100 = 3,200 seconds, about 53 minutes.
A server with a 10 Gbps NIC backs up 250 GB to a NAS on a 1 Gbps switch port. Roughly how long?

About 33 minutes.
250 GB x 8 = 2,000 Gb, / 1 Gbps = 2,000 s. The slowest link in the path sets the speed; the 10G NIC doesn't help.
